title: Climbing Mount PISA
author: Knowledge for Teachers
summary: Responding to Australia's declining PISA trajectory, Knowledge for Teachers argues the results themselves cannot diagnose the problem and instead builds a diagnostic framework around the four stages of the Instructional Hierarchy - acquisition, fluency, generalisation, and adaptation - that PISA's applied-reasoning tasks ultimately demand. The author identifies calm, focused classrooms as the non-negotiable precondition, then walks through specific classroom failure modes at each stage: teachers pre-sorting students before a lesson even starts, students never given real independent practice, concepts taught as memorised rules rather than must-have and can-have features, and problem-solving strategies left untaught entirely. A central metaphor, borrowed from Dr. Kent Johnson, frames fluency-building as shedding bricks from a backpack before attempting to climb Mount PISA's summit task of flexible, novel-problem adaptation. The piece closes on a call to intentionally align instruction with every stage of the hierarchy rather than leaving generalisation and adaptation to chance, summarized in the refrain that students cannot know what they were never explicitly taught.
points: Reframes falling PISA scores as an instructional-hierarchy diagnosis problem rather than a single-cause failure, arguing national test data can't localize the fix and only granular, school-level comparison can.

Names three specific, observable teacher behaviors that quietly block genuine skill acquisition: pre-sorting students by assumed ability before the lesson starts, ending practice when the bell rings rather than when independence is achieved, and unconsciously continuing to prompt students during supposed independent practice.

Uses Dr. Kent Johnson's backpack-of-bricks metaphor to make an abstract cognitive-load concept (extraneous load without fluency) into a concrete, teachable image: every increment of fluency is one brick removed before the real climb (generalisation and adaptation) can happen.

Distinguishes generalisation failure from acquisition failure precisely - explicit instruction can succeed at teaching a rule while still failing to teach when and how to apply it, because students are only taught 'what' concepts are, not their must-have and can-have features.

Ties adaptation specifically to Contingency Adduction - a named behavioral-science mechanism for spontaneously recombining mastered skills to solve novel problems - rather than treating 'transfer' as a vague aspiration.
quotes: The PISA assessment is like NAPLAN, it's an assessment that tests if students can generalise, apply, modify and adapt their skills and knowledge. Think of this ultimate goal of adaptation as summiting Mount PISA

The only way you can really get any information on what's working and not working is to get granular and look at individual schools that are bucking the trend and unpack what they are doing differently.

the teacher pre-allocates students into groups based on pre-conceived ideas of what students will be able to achieve before the lesson starts; the bell rings and so the teacher just moves onto the next lesson; the teacher doesn't realise that they are still heavily prompting the students when they think they are releasing responsibility onto the students by saying things like Don't forget to do this.

without fluency, it's like trying to scale Mount PISA with a bag of bricks on your back. Every time the learner is able to build fluency in something they're able to offload a brick from their backpack
we need to ensure students know the must-have and can-have features of a concept and when to apply principles, not just what they are
Contingency Adduction. This simply means a student can spontaneously combine separate skills they have already mastered to solve a brand new problem.
The title of this article really says it all. We cannot expect students to know what we do not teach them.
When we intentionally align our teaching with every single stage of learning, we stop leaving student success to chance.
context: Kent Johnson, frames fluency-building as shedding bricks from a backpack before attempting to climb Mount PISA's summit task of flexible, novel-problem adaptation.
